391.quote_or_event: “One does not attain liberation (merely) by the (study of) scripture, if he has no faith with regard to the nature of reality; or one who has faith cannot attain Nirvana if he is devoid of moral discipline.”
391.explanation: Kundakunda insists that scriptural learning is necessary but not enough. Knowledge has to be joined with right faith and lived out as right conduct, the three jewels of the Jain path.
391.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to learn flawlessly and then to stand firm in conduct worthy of what we have learned. Kundakunda says the same: learning without matching conduct does not reach the goal.
391.source: Pravacanasara III.237 (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)
391._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Upadhye's translation on jainworld.com, which numbers the verse 237. Very close on 'learn, then live accordingly', although the goal here is liberation and not worldly excellence.

392.quote_or_event: Jain texts say that Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara and first king, taught his daughter Brahmi the art of writing, so that the Brahmi script bears her name. He taught his other daughter Sundari the science of numbers (anka-vidya).
392.explanation: In Jain sacred history, letters and numbers are the first gifts of civilisation, handed down together by the first teacher of humankind to his two daughters.
392.tie_back: Valluvar calls numbers and letters the two eyes of every living person. The Jain story of Rishabha teaching Brahmi letters and Sundari numbers makes the same pair the foundation of all human learning.
392.source: Jain tradition on Rishabhanatha, Brahmi and Sundari, as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Rishabhanatha'
392._accuracy_note: The content is a striking, distinctly Jain match on 'letters and numbers'. However, it is paraphrased from Wikipedia as a last resort, because a primary-text page (Trishashti or Adipurana) could not be checked this session.

393.quote_or_event: “The saints have scriptures as their eyes; all the living beings have sense-organs as their eyes; the gods have clairvoyance as their eyes; and the Siddhas have eyes in every way.”
393.explanation: Kundakunda ranks kinds of 'eyes'. Ordinary beings see only with the senses, while the ascetic sees through scripture (agama-cakshu). The previous verse adds that a monk who lacks scriptural study 'does not know his self'.
393.tie_back: Valluvar says only the learned truly have eyes, and the unlearned carry two sores in their face. Kundakunda likewise treats learning as the real eye and sense-sight as the lowest kind of seeing.
393.source: Pravacanasara III.234 (cf. III.233) (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)
393._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Upadhye's translation on jainworld.com (verse 234). This is a near one-to-one use of the image of learning as the true eye, though the verse lacks the kural's harsh 'sores' contrast.

394.quote_or_event: “Sramanas, skilled in the interpretation of sacred texts and rich in moral discipline, austerities and right knowledge, should be welcomed with a stand-up, should be served and be bowed down to by other ascetics.”
394.explanation: Kundakunda tells monks to rise to their feet, serve and bow when a learned ascetic arrives. Meeting someone rich in knowledge is treated as an occasion for warm and respectful welcome.
394.tie_back: Valluvar describes the learned as those whose company gladdens others and whose parting leaves people longing to meet again. The Jain rule of joyful, reverent welcome expresses the same regard, although it does not mention the longing after they leave.
394.source: Pravacanasara III.263 (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)
394._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com (verse 263). This is a next-best fit: it prescribes honour for the learned, but it is a monastic etiquette rule, not a description of the delight and longing their company creates.

395.quote_or_event: “He who always acknowledges his allegiance to his teacher, who has religious zeal and ardour for study, who is kind in words and actions, deserves to be instructed.”
395.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana makes humble devotion to one's teacher, and staying in the teacher's lineage (kula), the condition for receiving learning. Its first lecture is devoted entirely to a disciple's humility (vinaya).
395.tie_back: Valluvar says those who stand humbly before their teachers, eager as the poor before the rich, are the superior ones. The Jain text likewise names lowly allegiance to the teacher as what makes a student worthy of instruction.
395._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on humble eagerness before the teacher, but it lacks the kural's poor-before-the-rich image and its condemnation of those who refuse to learn.

396.quote_or_event: “By study he destroys the Karman which obstructs right knowledge.”
396.explanation: In Jain doctrine, knowledge is the soul's own nature, only covered over by knowledge-obscuring karma (jnanavaraniya). Study wears that covering away, so understanding grows as more of the soul's latent knowledge is uncovered.
396.tie_back: Valluvar's well in the sand yields water the deeper it is dug, and knowledge wells up in proportion to learning. In the Jain picture, too, knowledge is already present and comes out more fully the more one studies.
396._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The doctrinal match is strong, since both describe knowledge emerging in proportion to study, but the Jain verse has no well image.

397.quote_or_event: “The enlightened and liberated monk should control himself, whether he be in a village or a town, and he should preach to all the road of peace; Gautama, &c.”
397.explanation: The Jain monk is homeless and keeps moving. Wherever his wandering takes him, village or town, he lives by the same discipline and shares his learning with everyone, and the refrain urges him to stay vigilant all his life.
397.tie_back: Valluvar says every land and every town belongs to the learned, so no one should stop learning until death. The Jain ideal of the wandering learned monk, at home and of use in any village or town, matches the first half of the kural.
397._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a partial, next-best fit. The 'any village or town' idea matches, but the verse is about the monk's conduct and preaching, not about learning making every place one's own.

398.quote_or_event: “By possession of knowledge he acquires an understanding of words and their meaning; thereby he will not perish in the forest of the fourfold Saṃsâra; as a needle with its thread will not be lost, thus the soul possessing the sacred lore will not be lost in the Saṃsâra.”
398.explanation: Mahavira's teaching plays on sutta, meaning both 'thread' and 'scripture'. A needle with a thread is not lost, and a soul that holds sacred knowledge is not lost in the cycle of rebirths.
398.tie_back: Valluvar says learning gained in one birth protects a person through seven births to come. The Jain image of the threaded needle makes the same promise: knowledge keeps the soul safe across the round of rebirth.
398._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a near one-to-one parallel on learning protecting the soul across many births. The Jain framing aims at final release, not only at protection in future lives.

399.quote_or_event: “Therefore, seeker after the highest truth, study the sacred lore, in order to cause yourself and others to attain perfection.”
399.explanation: The lecture on 'the very learned' ends by saying that learning is pursued for one's own good and for the good of others alike. What perfects the learner should also benefit the world.
399.tie_back: Valluvar says the learned love learning all the more when they see that it delights the world as well as themselves. The Jain verse likewise ties one's own study to the good it brings to others.
399._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on learning that serves both self and others, although the kural's emphasis on growing delight is not explicit.

400.quote_or_event: “As the ocean of inexhaustible water, the delight of Svayambhû, which is full of precious things of many kinds, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
400.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana ends its praise of the learned by comparing them to an inexhaustible ocean full of precious things. An earlier verse in the same lecture (11.26) compares them to 'a well-guarded storehouse … filled with grain of many kinds'.
400.tie_back: Valluvar calls learning the one imperishable wealth, beside which all else is not wealth. The Jain images of an inexhaustible, treasure-filled ocean and a well-guarded storehouse present learning as unequalled and undiminishing riches in the same way.
400._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Good thematic fit (inexhaustible riches, no equal), but it is a simile, not an explicit claim that learning alone is true wealth.
